title: Groups of Order p² are Abelian — the Full Structural Dichotomy
description: Every group of order p² is abelian, and moreover is either cyclic (≅ ℤ/p²) or elementary abelian of exponent p (≅ ℤ/p × ℤ/p). This entry supplies the order-dichotomy on elements that separates the two isomorphism types — the content Mathlib's single abelian lemma leaves implicit.

originalContributions: Structural dichotomy `isCyclic_or_pow_prime_eq_one`: a group of order p² is either cyclic or satisfies g^p = 1 for every element — the element-order split, obtained from Lagrange (orderOf g ∈ {1, p, p²}), that Mathlib does not package
Maximal-order characterization `isCyclic_iff_exists_orderOf_eq`: such a group is cyclic exactly when some element attains the full order p²

Elementary-abelian branch `exponent_eq_prime_of_not_isCyclic`: the non-cyclic case has exponent exactly p (not 1, since the group is nontrivial), identifying it as (ℤ/p)² together with the abelian result
Frames Mathlib's `IsPGroup.commutative_of_card_eq_prime_sq` as the base of the ℤ/p² vs (ℤ/p)² classification rather than an endpoint

overview.historicalContext: That every group of order $p^2$ is abelian is one of the earliest structural theorems of finite group theory, established in the p-group program of the late 19th century and given its definitive treatment in Burnside's *Theory of Groups of Finite Order* (1897). The engine is the class equation, itself a descendant of Sylow's 1872 theorems on prime-power subgroups: for a nontrivial finite p-group the sum of conjugacy-class sizes forces $p \mid |Z(G)|$, so the centre is never trivial. For $|G| = p^2$ this immediately yields commutativity, because a group with cyclic central quotient is abelian. Combined with the structure theorem for finite abelian groups — the culmination of work by Kronecker, Frobenius, and Stickelberger in the 1870s–1880s — one obtains that a group of order $p^2$ is isomorphic to exactly one of $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ or $\mathbb{Z}/p \times \mathbb{Z}/p$. Modern textbooks (Dummit–Foote §6.1) present this as the first nontrivial classification a student meets. Mathlib packages only the abelian half as `IsPGroup.commutative_of_card_eq_prime_sq`; this entry supplies the element-order invariant that completes the classification.
overview.problemStatement: Let $G$ be a group with $|G| = p^2$ for a prime $p$. Prove that $G$ is abelian, and pin down the invariant that separates its two isomorphism types: $G$ is either cyclic ($\cong \mathbb{Z}/p^2$, i.e. some element has order $p^2$) or every element $g$ satisfies $g^p = 1$, making $G$ elementary abelian of exponent $p$ ($\cong \mathbb{Z}/p \times \mathbb{Z}/p$).
overview.proofStrategy: The class equation gives a nontrivial centre $Z$, forcing $|Z| \in \{p, p^2\}$; if $|Z| = p$ then $G/Z$ has order $p$ and is cyclic, and a group with cyclic central quotient is abelian, so $G$ is abelian in every case (this is Mathlib's `commutative_of_card_eq_prime_sq`). The remaining, genuinely new content is the isomorphism-type split, extracted purely from Lagrange: the order of any $g$ divides $p^2$, hence equals $p^m$ with $m \le 2$. A clean case analysis follows — if some $\operatorname{ord}(g) = p^2$ then $g$ generates $G$ and $G$ is cyclic; otherwise every $\operatorname{ord}(g) \mid p$, so $g^p = 1$ for all $g$. The non-cyclic branch is then shown to have exponent exactly $p$ (dividing $p$ from the dichotomy, and $\ne 1$ since $|G| = p^2 > 1$), identifying it as $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$.
keyInsights: **Mathlib stops at 'abelian'; the real content is the isomorphism type.** `IsPGroup.commutative_of_card_eq_prime_sq` proves commutativity but leaves implicit *which* abelian group of order $p^2$ one has. This entry supplies the missing separating invariant, turning a single lemma into a complete classification.

**Lagrange alone separates the two types.** No further structure theory is needed for the split: $\operatorname{ord}(g) \mid p^2 \Rightarrow \operatorname{ord}(g) \in \{1, p, p^2\}$. The existence of an order-$p^2$ element is exactly the boundary between cyclic and elementary abelian — a strikingly elementary criterion.

**A maximal-order element is a constructive witness for cyclicity.** `isCyclic_iff_exists_orderOf_eq` reduces 'is $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/p^2$?' to the concrete search for an element attaining order $p^2$, via `isCyclic_of_orderOf_eq_card`.

**The non-cyclic case has exponent exactly $p$, not merely dividing $p$.** The lower bound matters: `exponent_eq_prime_of_not_isCyclic` rules out exponent $1$ (which would make $G$ trivial, contradicting $|G| = p^2$), so the exponent is pinned to $p$ — the defining feature of an elementary abelian group $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$.

**The class equation is the hidden foundation.** The nontrivial-centre fact that drives the abelian result is a consequence of the same prime-power counting that underlies the Sylow theorems, tying this small classification to the general p-group machinery.

sections.title: Introduction: From 'abelian' to the isomorphism type
sections.summary: Module header explaining that Mathlib already proves groups of order p² are abelian, and that the genuine remaining content — packaged here — is the element-order dichotomy that separates ℤ/p² from (ℤ/p)².
sections.mathContext: Every finite $p$-group has nontrivial centre (class equation). For $|G| = p^2$ this yields abelian. The structure theorem splits abelian order-$p^2$ groups into $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ and $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$; the separating invariant is whether an element of order $p^2$ exists.

sections.title: Groups of order p² are abelian
sections.summary: Exposes Mathlib's `IsPGroup.commutative_of_card_eq_prime_sq` as the base of the classification.
sections.mathContext: $|G| = p^2 \Rightarrow \forall a\,b,\ ab = ba$, via nontrivial centre and the 'central quotient cyclic $\Rightarrow$ abelian' principle.

sections.title: The structural dichotomy
sections.summary: Main result: a group of order p² is either cyclic or has every element satisfying g^p = 1, proved from Lagrange via the possible element orders 1, p, p².
sections.mathContext: $\operatorname{ord}(g) \mid p^2 \Rightarrow \operatorname{ord}(g) = p^m,\ m \le 2$. $m = 2 \Rightarrow$ cyclic; $m \le 1 \Rightarrow \operatorname{ord}(g) \mid p \Rightarrow g^p = 1$.

sections.title: Cyclic ⇔ maximal-order element; the elementary-abelian branch
sections.summary: Cyclicity is equivalent to the existence of an element of order p², and in the non-cyclic case the exponent is exactly p, identifying (with abelian) the group as (ℤ/p)².
sections.mathContext: Non-cyclic $\Rightarrow$ exponent $\mid p$; exponent $\ne 1$ since $|G| = p^2 > 1$; hence exponent $= p$.

conclusion.summary: Groups of order $p^2$ are not merely abelian: they fall into exactly two isomorphism types, $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ and $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$, separated by whether an element of order $p^2$ exists. The dichotomy `isCyclic_or_pow_prime_eq_one` and the exponent computation `exponent_eq_prime_of_not_isCyclic` supply the element-order invariant that turns Mathlib's abelian lemma into a complete classification, fully machine-checked with no axioms or sorries.
conclusion.implications: This is the smallest non-abelian-order case that is nonetheless forced to be abelian, and the first genuine isomorphism-type classification in the p-group program. It illustrates a template used throughout finite group theory: derive commutativity from the class equation, then use element orders (Lagrange) and the structure theorem to separate isomorphism types. The formalized invariant — existence of a maximal-order element — is precisely the data a computer search or a downstream proof needs to decide the type, making the entry a reusable building block for classifying groups of order $p^3$, $pq$, and beyond.
openQuestions: Can the argument be extended to a fully formalized classification of groups of order $p^3$, where the abelian analysis is joined by two non-abelian types (Heisenberg mod $p$ and the extraspecial group of exponent $p^2$)?
Is there a uniform Lean lemma characterizing when a finite abelian p-group of order $p^n$ is cyclic versus of a given exponent, generalizing the $n = 2$ dichotomy proved here?
Could `isCyclic_iff_exists_orderOf_eq` and the exponent computation be upstreamed to Mathlib as the packaged order-$p^2$ classification, complementing the existing abelian lemma?
